case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the rule of Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 plaintiff from obtaining prospective declaratory or injunctive relief (especially First Amendment-related relief) when such relief would imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal conviction that has not been reversed or otherwise favorably terminated.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (as limited by the implied favorable-termination requirement recognized in Heck v. Humphrey), with the underlying claims framed around the First Amendment (speech/assembly) and related requests for declaratory and injunctive relief against municipal enforcement policies.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Olivier argues that Heck’s favorable-termination bar should not apply—at least not categorically—to claims for prospective relief (injunctions/declarations) aimed at preventing future enforcement of allegedly unconstitutional municipal policies; he contends that extending Heck beyond damages improperly insulates unconstitutional speech-related enforcement from judicial review, creates an overbroad obstacle to prospective First Amendment relief, and conflicts with the purposes of § 1983 and traditional equitable remedies.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Brandon argues that Heck applies here to foreclose Olivier’s suit (including prospective relief) because the requested relief would necessarily call into question the validity of his still-outstanding conviction; respondents also emphasize case-specific barriers independent of Heck—such as forfeiture/presentment problems and potential preclusion doctrines (estoppel/res judicata)—and note related Fifth Circuit developments (including Siders v. City of Brandon) suggesting this case is a poor vehicle and that even if Olivier prevailed on the Heck question, his claims could still fail on remand.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the best opposing-case point that Wilkinson and Skinner preserve a meaningful § 1983 lane for forward-looking relief and warn against insulating ongoing unconstitutional enforcement from review; I agree the rule cannot be categorical. But Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” and Edwards v. Balisok’s functional approach still require an as-pleaded inquiry into whether the specific decree would necessarily imply invalidity, and here Justice Barrett and Justice Alito persuasively explain that the requested declaration/injunction would negate an essential premise of the still-valid conviction rather than merely regulate future enforcement. Justice Sotomayor’s tailoring/preclusion proposal is attractive as a remedial matter, but under our minimal, precedent-focused methodology the threshold Heck question turns on what success on these pleadings would establish, not on how a court might later rewrite the requested relief. A narrow affirmance limited to these pleadings preserves Wilkinson/Skinner for properly framed prospective challenges while preventing § 1983 from becoming a habeas substitute in this case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Wilkinson and Skinner preserve a meaningful lane for prospective § 1983 relief and that courts can often tailor decrees to avoid trenching on a conviction. But under Heck’s necessary-implication test—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress—the threshold question is what success on these pleadings would establish, not what a court might later rewrite; here the requested declaration/injunction would negate an essential premise of the still-outstanding judgment and thus functions as a collateral attack Preiser and Balisok forbid outside habeas. Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” qualifier confirms that some equitable claims remain barred when they are incompatible with the conviction’s continued validity, and Skinner underscores that labels do not control when the logic of the requested relief would necessarily imply invalidity. I therefore remain with Respondent while leaving room for properly framed, genuinely prospective challenges that do not logically entail invalidity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that Wilkinson and Skinner preserve § 1983 for forward-looking relief and that we should not dilute Heck’s “necessarily imply” test into a broader “casts doubt” prudential bar. But the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett correctly focus the inquiry on the decree “as pleaded”: the declaration/injunction sought here would establish that petitioner’s past conduct was constitutionally protected and that the enforcement action leading to a still-valid conviction was unconstitutional, which in functional terms necessarily implies the conviction’s invalidity under Heck/Balisok. Justice Sotomayor’s tailoring/preclusion proposal is appealing as a remedial safety valve, yet it cannot cure a threshold jurisdictional/doctrinal problem when success on the claim, as framed, would itself negate an essential premise of the outstanding judgment—precisely the end-run around habeas finality and comity that Preiser and Heck aim to prevent. Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” qualifier matters because it leaves room for properly cabined prospective suits; it does not require us to treat this particular suit, which is logically incompatible with the conviction’s continued validity, as permissible under § 1983.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett raise the hardest point: that we must evaluate the requested decree “as pleaded,” and some forward-looking relief can, in its operative terms, necessarily negate an essential premise of an outstanding conviction. But that is precisely why the correct approach is the Wilkinson/Skinner remedy-specific “necessary implication” test, not an upfront favorable-termination rule that functionally treats any prospective First Amendment challenge as habeas-adjacent; Justice Kagan is right that collapsing “necessarily implies” into “effectively adjudicates” is unworkable and overbroad. Even taking Balisok seriously, the bar attaches only when the judgment entered would itself establish invalidity, and where pleadings are overinclusive, ordinary tailoring on remand (and preclusion doctrines) can protect finality without insulating ongoing enforcement practices that chill speech—especially for vulnerable speakers who will not risk repeated arrests to obtain review. Under my pragmatic, access-to-justice lens, we should not close the courthouse door when prospective relief can be crafted to regulate future conduct without adjudicating the conviction’s validity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s “as pleaded” point is the strongest for Respondent, and I agree Heck can reach equitable relief when the decree, by its own operative terms, necessarily negates an essential premise of an outstanding conviction. But that is exactly why the administrable line must remain Heck’s logical-necessity test, not Justice Alito’s broader “effectively adjudicate” framing that risks collapsing ‘necessarily implies’ into ‘casts doubt’ and thereby shrinking Wilkinson and Skinner’s preserved § 1983 lane for prospective relief. On these pleadings, the better course consistent with § 1983’s text and our remedial practice is to treat overbreadth as a tailoring/remand problem (with preclusion doing its ordinary work), rather than a threshold favorable-termination bar that would functionally insulate forward-looking challenges whenever they overlap factually with a conviction. Chief Justice Roberts’s minimal affirmance proposal still turns too much on the plaintiff’s initial phrasing and invites strategic pleading fights, whereas a decree-focused “necessary implication” inquiry (as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes) preserves finality without converting Heck into a general prudential abstention for prospective constitutional claims.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s “as pleaded” point squarely presents the hardest Heck problem: we cannot allow artful requests for declaratory/injunctive relief to function as a collateral attack on an outstanding conviction. But Heck’s rule, as Skinner and Wilkinson confirm, turns on logical necessity—whether the judgment sought would by its own terms establish the conviction’s invalidity—not on whether it would “effectively” undermine it in some broader, prudential sense (as Justice Alito’s formulation risks doing). Where relief can be crafted to regulate only future enforcement without negating an element essential to the conviction, § 1983’s text authorizing equitable relief remains operative, and remedial tailoring plus ordinary preclusion doctrines address the end-run concern without expanding Heck into a freestanding courthouse-door bar. Because the respondent’s approach still tends to inflate “necessarily imply” into “strongly suggests,” I remain with petitioner while recognizing the decree must be limited to avoid any direct invalidation of the conviction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that Wilkinson and Skinner preserve § 1983 for genuinely prospective relief and that the line is logical necessity, not whether the judgment would merely “cast doubt” on the conviction. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly focus the inquiry on the decree actually sought: on these pleadings, a declaration/injunction would establish that the conduct underlying the still-valid conviction was constitutionally protected or that the enforcement was unconstitutional in a way that negates an essential premise of the judgment, which necessarily implies invalidity under Heck/Balisok regardless of the “prospective” label. Justice Sotomayor’s tailoring/remand approach is appealing as a practical matter, but under our institutionalist, precedent-first methodology we cannot evade the threshold Heck inquiry by hypothesizing narrower relief not requested; Skinner itself reinforces that remedy labels do not control when success is logically incompatible with the conviction’s continued validity. A narrow affirmance limited to these pleadings preserves room for future § 1983 challenges that truly can coexist with an outstanding conviction while preventing an end-run around Preiser/Heck finality and comity here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor most strongly press that Wilkinson and Skinner preserve § 1983 for forward-looking relief and that any overbreadth can be handled through tailoring or preclusion rather than a threshold Heck bar. But Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” and Heck’s own necessary-implication test require us to ask what success on the claim as pleaded would establish; here, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the requested declaration/injunction would negate an essential premise of an outstanding conviction and thus functions as a collateral attack Preiser and Heck reserve to habeas absent favorable termination. Justice Gorsuch is right that the line is logical necessity rather than “casts doubt,” yet on this record the logical entailment runs the wrong way for petitioner: prevailing would necessarily establish the conviction’s constitutional defect. Tailoring may be appropriate in other cases, but under a textualist/originalist and precedent-faithful approach, it cannot substitute for the threshold inquiry when the decree sought itself would necessarily imply invalidity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “as pleaded” point is the most serious counterargument: Wilkinson’s “ordinarily” and Balisok confirm that equitable relief can be Heck-barred when the decree itself necessarily establishes the invalidity of an outstanding conviction. But I do not read the pleadings as inevitably demanding a judgment that negates an element of the conviction; consistent with Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s approach, the proper course is to ask whether effective prospective relief can be crafted to regulate future enforcement without adjudicating the constitutional validity of petitioner’s past conduct as a matter of logical necessity. Justice Barrett and Justice Alito treat the requested declaration/injunction as inherently incompatible with the conviction’s continued validity, but that risks collapsing Heck’s “necessarily imply” standard into a broader “casts doubt/effectively adjudicates” prudential screen that Skinner warns against and that would, as a practical consequence, insulate ongoing municipal policies with continuing chilling effects. Given that ordinary tailoring, severability of remedies, and preclusion principles can protect finality/comity on remand, I do not think Heck should operate here as a threshold bar at the courthouse door.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination requirement reflects a finality-and-comity principle at the intersection of § 1983 and habeas, preventing § 1983 from functioning as a collateral attack on an outstanding conviction. While Wilkinson v. Dotson and related dicta (e.g., Edwards v. Balisok) indicate that prospective relief “ordinarily” will not necessarily imply invalidity, that qualifier matters: where the requested declaration or injunction would, as pleaded, negate an essential premise of the still-valid conviction, the suit falls within Heck’s “necessarily imply” bar. A narrow holding that turns on the particular relief sought—rather than a categorical rule about all prospective First Amendment injunctions—best preserves institutional legitimacy, respects precedent, and avoids inviting end-runs around state criminal judgments through § 1983.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983 supplies a cause of action, but it does not displace the traditional rule—reflected in habeas practice and recognized in Preiser v. Rodriguez—that a prisoner may not use § 1983 to obtain relief that would necessarily demonstrate the invalidity of an outstanding conviction or the fact or duration of custody. Heck v. Humphrey properly carried that principle into § 1983 by requiring favorable termination where success would necessarily imply invalidity; that logic applies regardless of whether the plaintiff styles the remedy as damages or declaratory/injunctive relief when the decree would, in substance, negate the conviction. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms the boundary: § 1983 remains available only when success would not necessarily imply invalidity, but Olivier’s requested prospective relief would undermine the still-valid judgment. Because the conviction has not been reversed or otherwise favorably terminated, the suit is barred under Heck’s necessary-implication rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey recognizes an implied favorable-termination requirement in 42 U.S.C. § 1983 to prevent civil actions from functioning as collateral attacks on outstanding criminal convictions, and that logic is not limited to damages when the requested relief would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity. Edwards v. Balisok confirms the doctrine’s reach turns on the necessary-implication inquiry, not the form of relief, and a declaration or injunction that the enforcement policy (as applied to petitioner’s conduct) is unconstitutional would call the still-valid conviction into question. While Wilkinson v. Dotson and Skinner v. Switzer allow some prospective § 1983 suits, they do so only where success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction or sentence; here, the prospective relief Olivier seeks is inseparable from the asserted invalidity of the very conviction that remains outstanding. Given finality and comity concerns, and the practical consequence of inviting end-runs around habeas limits, Heck’s bar should apply on these facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination requirement is properly understood as preventing § 1983 from being used as a substitute for habeas to invalidate an outstanding conviction or the duration of confinement, not as a categorical bar to forward-looking equitable relief aimed at preventing future unconstitutional enforcement. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, a § 1983 action may proceed where the requested declaratory or injunctive relief would not “necessarily imply” invalidity in the habeas sense—this Court has likewise recognized that an “otherwise proper injunction enjoining the prospective enforcement of invalid … regulations” is not barred. Extending Heck to foreclose prospective First Amendment relief would unduly insulate unconstitutional municipal policies from judicial review and disproportionately burden vulnerable speakers and protestors who most need access to equitable remedies under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. Any remaining vehicle or preclusion issues the City raises can be addressed on remand without expanding Heck beyond its doctrinal and equitable limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination requirement is best read as a limit on § 1983 suits that function as a collateral attack on an existing conviction—principally retrospective relief like damages—because it tracks common-law malicious-prosecution principles and the need for finality. Extending Heck to categorically bar forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief risks insulating ongoing, allegedly unconstitutional enforcement policies (including First Amendment restrictions) from any federal equitable review, a result difficult to square with § 1983’s remedial structure and workability. Edwards v. Balisok indicates Heck applies when relief “necessarily implies” invalidity, but it also suggests prospective relief “ordinarily” will not do so; the sound approach is to allow prospective claims unless the specific injunction/declaration would itself negate an essential element of the outstanding conviction. That narrower, text-and-function-based rule preserves coherence between § 1983 and habeas while still preventing end-runs around the conviction’s validity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey imposes a favorable-termination requirement only when success in the § 1983 action would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and this Court’s later decisions have confined that bar where the plaintiff seeks to use § 1983 as a functional substitute for habeas to undo a judgment. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and Edwards v. Balisok, forward-looking challenges to rules, policies, or procedures that govern future enforcement ordinarily remain cognizable under § 1983 because they do not necessarily render the prior conviction invalid, even if they cast doubt on the correctness of past proceedings. The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 authorizes suits for “equitable or other proper relief” against unconstitutional state action, and extending Heck to categorically foreclose prospective First Amendment injunctions would improperly expand an atextual limitation and risk insulating ongoing unconstitutional enforcement from judicial review. If, on the facts of a particular case, the requested declaration or injunction is framed so that it would directly negate an element essential to the existing conviction, ordinary doctrines of preclusion or narrow tailoring—not a categorical Heck extension—should do the work.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination rule bars § 1983 actions where success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and that principle should apply to equitable relief when the requested declaration or injunction would functionally negate the conviction’s legality. Wilkinson v. Dotson and Skinner v. Switzer confirm that § 1983 remains available for prospective relief only when success would not necessarily invalidate the conviction or shorten custody, but Olivier’s requested relief (as framed) would call the conviction itself into question. History and practical workability counsel against allowing § 1983 to become a de facto collateral attack on unreversed state judgments, which is the concern Heck addressed by channeling such disputes to habeas-type mechanisms. Given the case-specific vehicle problems noted (including potential forfeiture and preclusion issues), restraint and adherence to Heck’s core finality rationale favor affirmance here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1983’s text creates a cause of action for deprivation of federal rights, but Heck v. Humphrey supplies an implied limitation where the requested relief would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding criminal judgment absent favorable termination. Although Heck arose in a damages posture, its rationale—preventing a collateral attack on a still-valid conviction through § 1983 rather than habeas—tracks Preiser v. Rodriguez’s boundary and applies with equal force when a declaratory or injunctive decree would functionally negate the conviction’s validity. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that § 1983 remains available for prospective relief only when success would not necessarily demonstrate the invalidity of the conviction or shorten confinement; here, by hypothesis, the requested prospective relief would imply invalidity, so Heck bars the suit unless and until the conviction is set aside. This approach maintains methodological consistency and respects precedent while leaving room for § 1983 prospective claims that regulate future enforcement without undermining an extant judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey’s favorable-termination rule arose in the context of § 1983 damages actions that would function as an impermissible collateral attack on a conviction, and it should not be extended categorically to bar forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief aimed at preventing future enforcement of allegedly unconstitutional municipal policies. Where the plaintiff seeks prospective relief—particularly to protect First Amendment speech and assembly—procedural fairness and practical consequences weigh against insulating potentially unconstitutional enforcement from any meaningful federal review solely because a conviction remains outstanding. Spencer v. Kemna’s separate opinions underscore that rigidly applying Heck outside its core damages/malicious-prosecution analog risks leaving some plaintiffs without a forum, and that concern is heightened when the requested relief regulates future conduct rather than retroactively invalidating a judgment. The proper course is to allow prospective claims to proceed unless the relief would operate as the functional equivalent of habeas (i.e., necessarily produce immediate or speedier release), a line consistent with § 1983’s remedial purpose and this Court’s habeas/§ 1983 boundary cases.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 plaintiff from pursuing prospective declaratory and injunctive relief challenging a city’s enforcement practices when the plaintiff has an outstanding criminal conviction arising from the same events.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (and the Heck v. Humphrey favorable-termination doctrine as a limit on § 1983), with underlying First Amendment implications (speech/assembly) and Article III prospective-relief requirements (standing/ripeness) implicated by the requested injunction/declaration.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that Heck’s favorable-termination rule should not categorically preclude suits seeking forward-looking relief (declaratory/injunctive) against ongoing or threatened enforcement of allegedly unconstitutional municipal policies, because such relief does not necessarily imply the invalidity of an existing conviction and because barring prospective relief would leave individuals unable to prevent repeated future constitutional violations absent first overturning a conviction (a mismatch with § 1983’s remedial purpose and traditional equity practice).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that petitioner’s requested prospective relief is effectively an improper collateral attack on an outstanding conviction (and would, in substance or necessary effect, call that conviction into question), so Heck bars the suit; and even apart from Heck, the case is a poor vehicle due to additional barriers noted in the record such as forfeiture/presentment problems and other preclusion-like defenses (e.g., estoppel/res judicata), with related Fifth Circuit litigation (including Siders v. City of Brandon) underscoring that remand would not resolve the dispute cleanly.
key_precedents: Siders v. City of Brandon, Mississippi (5th Cir. Dec. 11, 2024)
Olivier v. City of Brandon (5th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press a serious point from Wilkinson and Skinner: Heck is not categorical and requires a claim- and remedy-specific inquiry focused on whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity. But as Justice Alito emphasizes, the particular declaration and injunction sought here cannot be granted without a judicial determination that the enforcement episode producing an outstanding conviction was unconstitutional, and that determination would in practical operation negate the conviction’s continuing legal validity—bringing this case within Heck’s favorable-termination boundary. Justice Sotomayor’s suggestion to rely on Article III, preclusion, and equitable tailoring is not an adequate substitute for that administrable habeas-channeling line recognized in Preiser and implemented by Heck; those doctrines are too contingent to prevent § 1983 from becoming a de facto vehicle for collateral review on these facts. Given my minimalist approach, I would decide narrowly that this specific requested relief crosses Heck’s line, leaving room for a cleaner case (or a narrower remand posture) where genuinely forward-looking relief can be severed from adjudicating the predicate illegality of the conviction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are right to insist that Heck uses a claim-by-claim “necessarily imply” inquiry, and Wilkinson and Skinner reject a categorical bar based on factual overlap alone. But the Chief Justice and Justice Alito correctly focus on what this plaintiff’s particular declaration and injunction would require: a judicial determination that the very enforcement episode supporting an outstanding conviction was unconstitutional, which as a matter of law necessarily negates the conviction’s continuing validity rather than merely “casting doubt” on it. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Article III limits, preclusion, and equitable tailoring cannot substitute for the structural habeas-channeling boundary of Preiser and Heck, because those doctrines do not prevent a federal equitable decree from operating as collateral review when the predicate finding is unavoidable. Under an originalist and textualist approach faithful to the habeas/§1983 division as this Court has articulated it, the relief sought here crosses Heck’s favorable-termination line even if narrower, truly prospective relief might be possible in a different posture.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are right to insist, citing Wilkinson and Skinner, on a claim-by-claim inquiry keyed to whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity, and I accept that Heck is not a categorical bar to all prospective relief. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas correctly identify that the particular declaration and injunction sought here cannot be awarded without a federal court adjudicating unconstitutional the enforcement episode that supplies the still-operative basis for the conviction, which necessarily undermines the conviction’s continuing legal validity in the way Heck and Preiser were designed to prevent. Justice Sotomayor’s proposed reliance on Article III limits, preclusion, and equitable tailoring is not an adequate substitute for Heck’s administrable favorable-termination boundary because it invites precisely the collateral relitigation of constitutional predicates that habeas-channeling is meant to avoid. Wilkinson is distinguishable because success there altered only future parole procedures while leaving the conviction and sentence intact; here, success necessarily condemns the predicate enforcement in a manner that functionally negates the judgment’s lawful foundation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito make the strongest respondent point on administrability: that the particular declaration/injunction could operate as a collateral attack by requiring a finding that the predicate enforcement episode was unconstitutional. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize via Wilkinson and Skinner, Heck turns on logical necessity—whether success would "necessarily imply" invalidity—not on factual overlap, stigma, or practical discomfort, and that limiting language is what keeps habeas-channeling from becoming de facto immunity for ongoing unconstitutional practices. If, as Justice Thomas worries, a specific theory of relief would negate an element essential to the outstanding conviction, Heck bars that slice; the proper response is remedy-by-remedy narrowing and equitable tailoring, not a categorical prohibition on prospective relief. I therefore remain with petitioner because a forward-looking decree can be framed to regulate future enforcement without adjudicating the past conviction’s unlawfulness, preserving finality while still providing access to justice for recurrent harms.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito offer the strongest administrability concern: that the particular declaration/injunction sought would require pronouncing unconstitutional the very enforcement episode underlying an outstanding conviction, and thus operate as collateral review. But as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Heck’s doctrinal trigger—confirmed by Wilkinson and Skinner—is not factual overlap or “practical stigma,” but whether success on the specific claim and remedy would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity; that limiting principle is administrable through a remedy-by-remedy analysis that bars any theory negating an element essential to the conviction while allowing genuinely prospective relief that regulates future enforcement without that logical entailment. Roberts’s suggestion to decide narrowly on this record is a serious caution, yet it cuts toward narrowing and tailoring (or remand to test severability), not toward expanding Heck into a categorical bar whenever the requested decree references the same enforcement episode. Thomas’s structural habeas-channeling point is answered by enforcing Heck where necessity exists, while preserving § 1983’s textually broad remedial scope for forward-looking relief that does not, as a matter of logic, invalidate the judgment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito offer the strongest respondent point: that this particular forward-looking decree would, in practical operation, require a court to pronounce unconstitutional the very enforcement episode underpinning an outstanding conviction and thus resemble collateral review. But Heck’s line—reinforced by Justice Kagan’s reliance on Wilkinson and Skinner—is not “practical overlap” or “stigmatization”; it is whether success would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity, a logical-entailment test that does not permit us to expand atextually into a categorical bar on prospective relief. Justice Thomas is right to worry about end-runs around habeas, yet that concern is addressed by slicing off (or narrowing) any theory or remedy that would negate an element essential to the conviction, while allowing truly prospective relief that can be granted without adjudicating the conviction’s unlawfulness. Under a textualist, precedent-bound approach, administrability cannot justify enlarging Heck beyond its necessity-based trigger when traditional equitable limits and claim-by-claim analysis can do the needed work.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that this requested declaration/injunction may, in practical operation, function as a collateral attack on an outstanding conviction—rightly focuses us on substance over labels, and I share the institutional concern about end-runs around habeas. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, Wilkinson and Skinner require a claim-by-claim, remedy-by-remedy inquiry keyed to whether success would necessarily imply invalidity; “practical overlap” or “stigma” is not the doctrinal test, and expanding Heck beyond its necessity standard would be an unwarranted, administrability-driven extension. The better precedent-respecting course is to allow only genuinely forward-looking relief that can be framed without adjudicating the past conviction’s unlawfulness, while directing lower courts to dismiss or narrow any theory that would negate an element essential to the existing conviction. That tailoring approach addresses Roberts’s collateral-attack concern through Article III and equitable limits without converting Heck into a categorical shield against prospective challenges to ongoing enforcement practices.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justices Thomas and Alito press the most serious concern: that the particular declaration/injunction sought would effectively adjudicate the unconstitutionality of the very enforcement episode supporting an outstanding conviction. But Heck’s operative limit, as Justice Kagan emphasizes via Wilkinson and Skinner, is a claim- and remedy-specific inquiry into whether success would “necessarily imply” invalidity, not whether the relief would practically “stigmatize” the conviction or share factual overlap. Under that framework, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that some formulations of relief here may be impermissibly backward-looking; the correct response is to bar or narrow any theory that would negate an element essential to the conviction, while permitting genuinely prospective relief that can be granted without that logical entailment. Expanding Heck into an administrability-driven categorical rule would depart from its textually anchored necessity standard and, as Justice Sotomayor notes, risk insulating ongoing enforcement practices from review where no necessary implication of invalidity exists.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s administrability point—that this particular declaration/injunction may, in practical operation, become a de facto collateral attack—is the most serious concern, and it underscores the need for disciplined remedial tailoring. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes via Wilkinson and Skinner, Heck’s boundary is logical necessity: whether success on the specific § 1983 claim and remedy would necessarily imply the conviction’s invalidity, not whether the relief would stigmatize the enforcement episode or share factual predicates. Justice Thomas is right that any portion of the requested relief that requires a finding negating an element essential to the outstanding conviction must be barred under Heck, but that does not justify a categorical rule insulating ongoing practices from forward-looking regulation where a court can grant relief without adjudicating the conviction’s unlawfulness. Article III constraints and equitable narrowing are not a substitute for Heck; they are the tools that, together with a remedy-by-remedy Heck inquiry, prevent backdoor relitigation while preserving § 1983’s role in addressing continuing constitutional harms.

John Roberts.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey requires dismissal of a § 1983 action when success would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and the requested declaration and injunction here—aimed at the city’s enforcement practices arising from the same events—risk functioning as an impermissible collateral attack on that still-valid conviction. Wilkinson v. Dotson confirms that prospective relief may proceed under § 1983 only when it would not necessarily spell invalidity of the conviction or sentence; this case, as framed, appears too intertwined with the conviction to satisfy that limiting principle. Given the institutional need for a narrow, administrable rule and to avoid using § 1983 to circumvent habeas-like favorable-termination requirements, I would affirm dismissal under Heck (or at minimum avoid a broad pro-petitioner ruling and leave any clarification for a cleaner vehicle). Federalism and Article III constraints on prospective relief further counsel against reopening state criminal judgments indirectly through federal equitable decrees.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1983 cannot be used as an end-run around the habeas boundary recognized in Preiser v. Rodriguez and the favorable-termination principle of Heck v. Humphrey when the requested relief would, in necessary practical effect, call into question an outstanding criminal judgment arising from the same events. While Wilkinson v. Dotson permits some forward-looking relief where success would not necessarily imply invalidity, the injunction and declaration sought here would effectively brand the enforcement that produced the conviction as unconstitutional and thereby undermine the conviction’s validity. The Constitution’s original meaning and the statutory text do not authorize federal courts to issue equitable relief that functions as collateral review of state criminal judgments outside the channels Congress has provided. Accordingly, Heck bars this § 1983 action to the extent it would necessarily impugn the existing conviction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits § 1983 when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and a declaratory judgment or injunction targeting the same enforcement actions that produced petitioner’s conviction functions in substance as a collateral attack on that conviction. Even if framed as forward-looking, the requested relief would effectively declare the underlying enforcement unconstitutional and thereby cast substantial doubt on the conviction’s validity, bringing the claim within Heck’s practical and doctrinal boundary. Wilkinson v. Dotson does not compel a different result because it involved parole procedures where success would not necessarily undermine the conviction or sentence; here, the challenged municipal enforcement practices are intertwined with the adjudicated criminal conduct. Given § 1983’s text and the need to avoid end-runs around habeas and finality interests central to Heck, I would affirm the bar at least where the prospective relief is inseparable from the validity of the existing conviction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits § 1983 only when success in the civil action would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction or sentence, a boundary this Court reaffirmed in Wilkinson v. Dotson, 544 U.S. 74, 81–82 (2005). A request for prospective declaratory and injunctive relief aimed at ongoing or threatened enforcement practices can be litigated without negating a past conviction, so long as the remedy is forward-looking and does not require a finding that the conviction itself was unlawful. Extending Heck to categorically bar prospective relief would misalign § 1983’s remedial purpose—especially for individuals facing recurring enforcement—by forcing vulnerable speakers to either endure repeated violations or first obtain favorable termination, which may be practically inaccessible. Article III limits (standing/ripeness) and ordinary preclusion doctrines can police improper collateral attacks, but Heck should not be expanded to foreclose equitable relief that does not necessarily undermine the conviction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 action only when success would "necessarily imply" the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, a limit rooted in channeling collateral attacks into habeas. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and Skinner v. Switzer, forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief aimed at changing future enforcement practices can proceed under § 1983 when it would not automatically negate the prior conviction or shorten its duration. The requested prospective relief here is not categorically a collateral attack; courts should apply Heck claim-by-claim and remedy-by-remedy, dismissing only those requests whose necessary effect would be to invalidate the conviction while leaving room for otherwise proper prospective relief consistent with traditional equity and § 1983’s remedial design. Article III workability concerns (standing/ripeness) can screen overbroad injunctions without expanding Heck beyond its "intersection" with habeas.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1983’s text creates a cause of action against any person who, under color of state law, deprives another of federal rights, and Heck v. Humphrey imposes only a narrow, judicially crafted limit where success in the § 1983 action would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson, a plaintiff may pursue declaratory and injunctive relief so long as the requested forward-looking remedy would not necessarily invalidate the existing conviction or shorten its duration; an injunction against future enforcement “does not work backwards” to nullify past judgments. Treating all prospective challenges to enforcement practices as barred would improperly expand Heck beyond its rationale (protecting habeas’s domain) and risk insulating potentially unconstitutional enforcement policies from review, contrary to traditional equity practice and Article III’s case-or-controversy limits (which can be handled through standing/ripeness rather than a categorical Heck bar). The proper rule is case-specific: only claims whose success would necessarily negate an element or validity of the conviction are barred, while purely prospective relief aimed at future conduct may proceed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey limits § 1983 only when the claim’s success would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction, and that principle—reaffirmed in Wilkinson v. Dotson and Skinner v. Switzer—does not categorically foreclose forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief aimed at preventing future enforcement of an allegedly unconstitutional municipal practice. Where the requested relief can be framed and administered prospectively without negating an element of the prior conviction, extending Heck would go beyond its historic habeas-channeling function and create serious practical and institutional problems by insulating ongoing unconstitutional enforcement from equitable review. The proper course is to allow prospective claims to proceed subject to ordinary Article III limits (standing, ripeness) and traditional equitable discretion, rather than an overbroad Heck bar. Any narrower preclusion or vehicle concerns can be addressed on remand without expanding Heck’s favorable-termination doctrine.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1983’s text creates a cause of action against state actors for ongoing or threatened deprivations of federal rights, and Heck v. Humphrey limits that remedy only when success in the civil action would “necessarily imply the invalidity” of an outstanding conviction. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson’s clarification of the “necessarily implies” inquiry, forward-looking declaratory or injunctive relief directed at future enforcement practices is not categorically barred, so long as the requested relief can be granted without negating an element essential to the existing conviction. Treating all prospective relief as an impermissible collateral attack extends Heck beyond its common-law favorable-termination rationale and risks foreclosing traditional equitable relief against future constitutional violations. Any remaining concerns about re-litigating the conviction are better handled by tailoring relief and by Article III and preclusion doctrines, rather than a categorical Heck bar.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Heck v. Humphrey bars a § 1983 action only when success would “necessarily imply” the invalidity of an outstanding conviction, and this Court has emphasized that the inquiry turns on the logical implications of the claim, not a categorical rule against any suit touching the same events. Under Wilkinson v. Dotson and Skinner v. Switzer, prospective declaratory and injunctive relief remains available where the plaintiff challenges allegedly unconstitutional enforcement practices going forward and prevailing would not automatically negate the elements or validity of the prior conviction. A contrary approach would unnecessarily expand Heck beyond its comity-and-finality rationale and would, as a practical matter, deny meaningful forward-looking relief to individuals subject to repeated allegedly unconstitutional enforcement—an outcome in tension with § 1983’s remedial purpose and traditional equity. Article III limits (standing/ripeness) and ordinary preclusion doctrines can still screen improper or speculative requests for prospective relief without converting Heck into a blanket bar.
